record.original_question: For 0 <= beta < d, define the centered Hardy-Littlewood fractional maximal operator by M_beta f(x) = sup_{r>0} m(B(x,r))^{beta/d - 1} ∫_{B(x,r)} |f(y)| dy, and define the uncentered fractional maximal operator analogously by taking the supremum over balls that contain x. When 0 <= beta < 1 and q = d/(d-beta), is the map f -> |∇M_beta f| bounded from W^{1,1}(R^d) to L^q(R^d)? The same question is asked for the uncentered fractional maximal operator.

evidence.quote: For 0 ≤ β < d and f ∈ L1loc (Rd) we define the centered Hardy-Littlewood fractional maximal function Mβ f by Mβ f (x) = sup_{r>0} 1/m(B(x, r))^{1−β/d} ∫_{B(x,r)} |f(y)| dy. When β = 0 we plainly recover (1.1). The uncentered fractional maximal function is defined analogously, with the supremum of the fractional averages being taken over balls that simply contain the point x, but are not necessarily centered at x.
Question 7. Let 0 ≤ β < 1 and q = d/(d − β). Is the map f → |∇Mβ f| bounded from W 1,1 (Rd) to Lq (Rd)? Same question for the uncentered version.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $d\ge 1$ be an integer. For a locally integrable function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ and $0\le\beta<d$, define the centered Hardy–Littlewood fractional maximal function by
$$M_\beta f(x)=\sup_{r>0}\frac{1}{m(B(x,r))^{1-\beta/d}}\int_{B(x,r)}|f(y)|\,dy,$$
where $m$ denotes Lebesgue measure and $B(x,r)$ is the open Euclidean ball of radius $r$ centered at $x$. Define the uncentered fractional maximal function $\widetilde{M}_\beta f(x)$ analogously, with the supremum taken over all open balls $B$ that contain $x$ (not necessarily centered at $x$):
$$\widetilde{M}_\beta f(x)=\sup_{B\ni x}\frac{1}{m(B)^{1-\beta/d}}\int_{B}|f(y)|\,dy.$$
Let $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ denote the Sobolev space of integrable functions whose distributional gradient is also integrable, with norm $\|f\|_{W^{1,1}}=\|f\|_{L^1}+\|\nabla f\|_{L^1}$.

Fix $0\le\beta<1$ and set $q=d/(d-\beta)$. Determine whether the map
$$f\;\longmapsto\;|\nabla M_\beta f|$$
is bounded from $W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ to $L^q(\mathbb{R}^d)$, i.e. whether there exists a constant $C=C(d,\beta)$ such that
$$\bigl\||\nabla M_\beta f|\bigr\|_{L^q(\mathbb{R}^d)}\le C\,\|f\|_{W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)}\qquad\text{for all }f\in W^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^d),$$
and answer the analogous question with $M_\beta$ replaced by the uncentered fractional maximal operator $\widetilde{M}_\beta$.
artifact.status_search_result: Beltran, Madrid, and others (Math. Z., 2022; arXiv:2010.05561) establish that for all $0<\alpha<d$ and $1\le p<d/\alpha$, both the centered and uncentered Hardy–Littlewood fractional maximal operators $\mathcal{M}_\alpha f$ are weakly differentiable on $W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with $\|\nabla\mathcal{M}_\alpha f\|_{p^*}\le C_{d,\alpha,p}\|\nabla f\|_p$, where $p^*=(p^{-1}-\alpha/d)^{-1}$, explicitly covering the previously unknown endpoint $p=1$ for $0<\alpha<1$ (with $W^{1,1}$ replaceable by BV). This affirmatively answers both the centered and uncentered versions of the question.

status_evidence.title: Endpoint Sobolev Bounds for Fractional Hardy-Littlewood Maximal Operators
status_evidence.snippet: both the centered and the uncentered Hardy-Littlewood fractional maximal operator M_alpha f are weakly differentiable and ||∇M_alpha f||_{p*} ≤ C ||∇f||_p ... In particular it covers the endpoint case p=1 for 0<alpha<1 where the bound was previously unknown.
status_evidence.claim: The endpoint W^{1,1} -> L^q bound for the gradient of the centered and uncentered fractional maximal operator with 0<alpha<1 and q=d/(d-alpha) is established in all dimensions.

status_evidence.title: Endpoint Sobolev bounds for fractional Hardy–Littlewood maximal operators (Math. Z., 2022)
status_evidence.snippet: Published version of the result establishing endpoint Sobolev bounds for centered and uncentered fractional Hardy–Littlewood maximal operators.
status_evidence.claim: The result has appeared in a peer-reviewed journal.
